rebirth.intro: Does anything carry on after death, and if so, what? The Buddha said a stream of becoming continues without a fixed self. The Upanishads said the Self is untouched while the subtle body moves on. Plato told the Myth of Er. Theosophy and Steiner rebuilt the idea for the modern West. Start anywhere and keep going.

practices.name: The five remembrances
practices.how: Each day, recollect slowly: I am subject to ageing; to illness; to death; I will be parted from all that is dear; I am the owner of my actions, and will inherit them. Let each one sink in before the next.

practices.name: Mindfulness of death (maranasati)
practices.how: At nightfall and daybreak, reflect that death could come tonight or today from many causes, and ask whether any unskilful quality is still unabandoned. Let the urgency feed effort, not fear.

practices.name: Recollecting the round
practices.how: Contemplate how long the round of birth and death has been, and how many losses it holds, until disenchantment with becoming arises. Then turn to the breath and rest.

practices.name: Powa: an introduction to transference at death
practices.how: Read a traditional introduction before seeking instruction from a qualified teacher: refuge, visualising Amitabha above the crown, and training the mind's direction at death. It is taught with empowerment, not from a page.

practices.name: Preparing for the bardo
practices.how: Notice the small gaps of daily life (falling asleep, the pause between thoughts) as rehearsals for the great transition, and rest there as awareness.
practices.src: Lion's Roar: The Fine Art of Conscious Dying (Glenn Mullin)

practices.name: Self-enquiry: who dies?
practices.how: When the thought of death comes, ask to whom it comes. Trace the 'I' back to its source instead of following the thought. Ramana's own awakening began by lying down and enacting his death.
practices.src: Who Am I? (Sri Ramanasramam, free PDF)

practices.name: Practising dying (melete thanatou)
practices.how: Socrates calls philosophy the practice of dying: loosening the soul's grip on the body's pleasures and fears, day by day. Read the Phaedo slowly as an exercise, not an argument.

practices.name: Self-enquiry
practices.how: Whenever a thought arises, ask to whom it arises; the answer is 'to me'; then ask 'who am I?' and hold attention on the sense of I.

practices.name: Contemplating not-self
practices.how: Take each aggregate in turn and ask: is it constant, is it easeful, is it fitting to regard it as me, mine, my self?

practices.name: Shiva Process self-inquiry
practices.how: Bring to mind a situation that is troubling you. Describe what you feel in plain words, then ask "what is the deeper feeling under this?" and keep going, layer by layer, until something shifts and the contraction releases. Often done in pairs or with a guide.

practices.name: "What am I? Don't know"
practices.how: Ask "What am I?" deeply on the in-breath. On the out-breath, hold "Don't know..." as long as the breath lasts. Return to this don't-know mind in every activity, and keep clear about the next correct action. This is Seung Sahn's Kwan Um teaching.

practices.name: Mindfulness of breathing
practices.how: Sit comfortably, know the in-breath and out-breath, then let the breath calm the whole body before turning to feelings and mind.

practices.name: Goodwill (metta)
practices.how: Wish yourself well, then widen the wish to others, near and far, seen and unseen, without exception.

practices.name: Resting in the gap between breaths (Vijñāna Bhairava dhāraṇā)
practices.how: Sit comfortably and breathe naturally. Notice the instant where the in-breath turns into the out-breath, and the instant where the out-breath turns back. Do not hold the breath; simply let attention fall into each turning point and rest there for its brief duration. Over time, notice the open awareness that is present in the pause.
practices.src: Bettina Bäumer, Vijñāna Bhairava verses 24–27 (the breath dhāraṇās).

practices.name: Recognition (pratyabhijñā) contemplation
practices.how: Read one sūtra of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam slowly. Then look at present experience — a sound, a thought, a feeling — and ask whether anything appears outside awareness. Let the understanding "this too is a form of the one consciousness" settle as a felt recognition rather than an idea. Return to the text, then to experience, alternating.
practices.src: Christopher Wallis on the twenty sūtras of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam.

practices.name: Drawing the Śrī Chakra as meditation
practices.how: Following a teacher's step-by-step construction, draw the Śrī Yantra slowly from the centre point (bindu) outward: the nine interlocking triangles, the lotus rings and the square gateways. Treat each stage as a contemplation of the goddess unfolding into the world, not as geometry homework.
practices.src: Devipuram, "How to Draw Sri Chakra" parts 1–2.

practices.name: Basic Śaiva Siddhānta meditation
practices.how: Sit upright, regulate the breath to a slow even count, then draw awareness inward from the senses to the spine and to the inner light, holding a single point of focus. Hinduism Today's monastery teaches it as part of daily worship and study.
practices.src: Bodhinatha Veylanswami, "How Do We Meditate? Part 1".

practices.name: Mantra repetition (japa)
practices.how: Choose a mantra received from your tradition, sit with a mala, and repeat it at an even pace, aloud, whispered or mentally. Let attention rest on the sound and its meaning; when the mind wanders, return to the next repetition.

practices.name: Ānāpānasati (breath meditation, "Method 2")
practices.trad: Dhammayut forest line (Ajahn Mun → Maha Boowa / Ajaan Lee)
practices.how: Sit upright and notice the breath at whatever point it is clearest. Let it settle into a comfortable rhythm, then let that sense of ease spread through the whole body, using the breath energy as a home base for steady, alert attention.

practices.name: "Buddho" recollection
practices.how: Silently repeat "bud-" on the in-breath and "-dho" on the out-breath to anchor the mind; when the mind is calm, drop the word and stay with the knowing itself. Used widely in the Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah lines.

practices.name: Walking meditation (jongrom)
practices.trad: Ajahn Chah line (Wat Nong Pah Pong)
practices.how: Choose a straight path of 15–30 paces. Walk at a natural or slow pace, attention on the feet or the whole body; at each end, stop, turn, and re-collect before walking back.

practices.name: Mahasi noting
practices.how: Watch the rise and fall of the abdomen and give each event a soft mental label ("rising", "falling", "thinking", "hearing"), then return to the primary object; move to slow walking with labels for lifting, moving and placing.

practices.name: Natural awareness (right attitude)
practices.how: Instead of forcing focus on one object, relax and know whatever is being experienced, checking the attitude of the observing mind (craving, aversion, impatience) throughout daily activities.

practices.name: Satipaṭṭhāna (four establishings of mindfulness)
practices.how: Contemplate body, feeling, mind and mental qualities as they arise and pass, ardent, clearly knowing and mindful, without greed or distress about the world (MN 10).

practices.name: RAIN
practices.how: Recognise what is happening; Allow it to be there; Investigate with kindness how it feels in the body; Nurture with self-compassion; then rest in the awareness that remains.

practices.how: The sixteen steps, from the breath to release.

practices.name: Open awareness (shamatha without a support)
practices.how: After a few minutes with a support, let it go. Leave the eyes open and the gaze soft. Let sights, sounds and thoughts come and go, and do not follow them or push them away. When you get caught up, simply notice it and relax again. The point is to rest as the knowing that is already present.

practices.name: Looking at the mind (Mahamudra)
practices.how: Once the mind is calm, turn and look for the one who is looking. Ask where a thought comes from, where it stays, and where it goes. Do not reason about it; just look and rest in whatever is seen or not found. This practice is traditionally done under a qualified teacher's guidance.

practices.name: Resting in rigpa (Dzogchen), orientation only
practices.how: In Dzogchen, the student is introduced to the nature of mind (rigpa) by a teacher. Between sessions, practitioners recall that recognition, leave it uncontrived for short moments, many times, and release any effort to improve it. This entry describes the practice and is not a substitute for the introduction itself.

practices.name: Shikantaza (just sitting)
practices.how: Sit as in zazen, but drop counting and any object. Simply sit, aware of the whole posture and the whole field of experience, without chasing or suppressing anything. When you find yourself lost in thought, come back to the posture. Dogen treats the sitting itself as realisation, not as a means to it.

practices.name: Koan practice with Mu
practices.how: Take up "Does a dog have buddha nature? Mu" (Zhaozhou). Breathe Mu on each exhalation and put your whole doubt into it. Do not interpret it. Present your understanding to a teacher in private interview (dokusan). Koan work depends on that meeting with a teacher.

practices.name: Silent illumination (mozhao)
practices.how: Relax the body and be aware of the whole body sitting. Widen that awareness to include the environment, without any centre or edge. Silence means not adding commentary; illumination means remaining clearly aware. Rest there, and return whenever you get caught.

faith.intro: Devotion is the path of the heart: love turned toward the divine, a teacher, or a name. Bhakti sings it, Pure Land entrusts itself to Amida, the Sufi remembers God with every breath, the Christian prays without ceasing. Here the traditions describe what surrender is, and how it is practised.

practices.name: Bhairavi Sadhana (Isha)
practices.how: A lay devotional observance offered by the Isha Foundation around Linga Bhairavi: for a set period the practitioner keeps simple disciplines (as given by Isha), offers daily devotion to the goddess, and completes it with an offering at a Linga Bhairavi abode. The exact rules come from the organisation each year.

practices.name: "Buddho" recollection
practices.how: Silently repeat "bud-" on the in-breath and "-dho" on the out-breath to anchor the mind; when the mind is calm, drop the word and stay with the knowing itself. Used widely in the Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah lines.

practices.name: Śravaṇa–manana–nididhyāsana
practices.how: Systematic listening to the Upaniṣads with a teacher (śravaṇa), resolving doubts by reflection (manana), and dwelling on the understood meaning until it is assimilated (nididhyāsana).

practices.name: Japa (repetition of a divine name)
practices.how: Repeat a mantra or name of God given by the teacher, often with a mālā of 108 beads, letting the mind rest in its meaning and the feeling of devotion.

practices.name: Hare Krishna mahāmantra (japa and kīrtan)
practices.how: Chant "Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare / Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare" softly on beads (japa) or sing it together (kīrtan), as practised since Chaitanya.

practices.name: Nembutsu / nianfo
practices.how: Recite "Namu Amida Butsu" (Japanese) or "Namo Amituofo" (Chinese), aloud or silently, with a mala if you like. In Chinese Pure Land, recitation is a practice of concentration and aspiration for rebirth. In Shin Buddhism, it is an expression of gratitude for Amida's vow, not a means of earning anything.

practices.name: Christian meditation with a mantra (Maranatha)
practices.how: Sit still and upright with your eyes lightly closed. Silently repeat one prayer-word, "Ma-ra-na-tha", in four equal syllables, listening to it rather than thinking about its meaning. When thoughts or images arrive, return to the word, without force. Sit for 20–30 minutes, morning and evening.

practices.name: Centering Prayer
practices.how: Choose a sacred word as a sign of consent to God's presence. Sit comfortably and bring it in gently. When you notice you are engaged with a thought, return ever so gently to the word. End by resting in silence for a couple of minutes. Twice daily, 20 minutes.

practices.name: Lectio Divina
practices.how: Read a short scripture passage slowly, then again; notice the word that catches you; respond to it in prayer; rest in silence. Read, ponder, pray, rest.

practices.name: The Jesus Prayer (prayer of the heart)
practices.how: Repeat "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me" slowly and attentively, often with a prayer rope, keeping the mind in the words and letting it descend into the heart. Begin with a fixed time each day; humility and stillness come before technique.

practices.name: Zikr (remembrance) in the Inayati way
practices.how: Sitting quietly, repeat the phrase of divine unity (La ilaha illa'llah) aloud or silently, letting the breath and a gentle movement of the head carry it, until the remembrance continues on its own in the heart.

practices.name: Dhikr and breathwork
practices.how: Join a short divine name or phrase to the in- and out-breath; keep attention on the heart; finish with silence and a prayer.

practices.name: Khatm-i Khwajagan (Naqshbandi group dhikr)
practices.how: A set Naqshbandi litany of Qur'an recitation, blessings on the Prophet and silent or vocal remembrance, recited together under a shaykh's guidance.

practices.name: Weekly parashah reflection (neo-Hasidic)
practices.how: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

reality.intro: Not two. Advaita says the world is Brahman appearing as many; Kashmir Shaivism says it is consciousness recognising itself; Dzogchen and Zen point to a nature that was never divided; the philosophers of the sacred ask whether mind comes first. Here is nonduality, and the question of what is real.

practices.name: Recognition (pratyabhijñā) contemplation
practices.how: Read one sūtra of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam slowly. Then look at present experience — a sound, a thought, a feeling — and ask whether anything appears outside awareness. Let the understanding "this too is a form of the one consciousness" settle as a felt recognition rather than an idea. Return to the text, then to experience, alternating.
practices.src: Christopher Wallis on the twenty sūtras of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam.

practices.name: Calming and contemplation (zhiguan)
practices.how: First calm the mind (zhi) by settling the breath and posture. Then contemplate (guan) any present thought as simultaneously empty, provisionally existing, and the middle, which are the threefold truth. Zhiyi's Mohe zhiguan sets out four kinds of samadhi practice (constant sitting, constant walking, half-walking half-sitting, and neither).

self/emptiness.intro: Form is emptiness, emptiness is form. For the Madhyamaka, nothing exists from its own side; for Zen, emptiness is this very moment; for Thich Nhat Hanh, it is interbeing; for Dzogchen, it is the open ground of mind. Here the Buddhist schools, and a few outside them, explain what emptiness is and is not.

meditation/kundalini.intro: The subtle body: channels, centres and a coiled power at the base of the spine. Haṭha yoga, the tantras of Kashmir and the Goddess, Tibetan yogas and modern teachers describe it differently, and scholars trace where the idea came from. Here are the teachers, the history, and the cautions.

practices.name: Rudi's double breath
practices.how: Breathe in, bringing attention down from the throat into the heart, and then down to the navel and the base of the body. Breathing out, let the energy rise up the spine. Keep the movement gentle and continuous, and return to the heart when attention scatters.
practices.src: Swami Khecaranatha on Rudi's double breath.

practices.name: Drawing the Śrī Chakra as meditation
practices.how: Following a teacher's step-by-step construction, draw the Śrī Yantra slowly from the centre point (bindu) outward: the nine interlocking triangles, the lotus rings and the square gateways. Treat each stage as a contemplation of the goddess unfolding into the world, not as geometry homework.
practices.src: Devipuram, "How to Draw Sri Chakra" parts 1–2.

practices.name: Khecarī mudrā (historical description only)
practices.how: Described in haṭha texts as turning the tongue back and up into the cavity above the soft palate, sometimes after gradually lengthening the tongue. We list it for context: the full form involves cutting the frenum and is not something to try from a video.
practices.src: Mallinson, The Khecarīvidyā (DPhil); no short clip on file.

imaginal.intro: Between the world of the senses and the world of pure ideas lies a third: the imaginal, Henry Corbin's word for the realm where visions, angels and archetypes are real. Sufis, Renaissance Platonists, Jung and Hillman, and today's scholars of myth and cosmology explore it. Here is imagination taken seriously.

practices.name: Dream yoga, first steps
practices.how: During the day, keep reminding yourself "this is a dream" so that the habit carries into sleep. Before sleep, set a strong intention to recognise dreams. Visualise a luminous syllable at the throat as you fall asleep. Each morning, review whether you recognised a dream, and renew the intention.

practices.name: Feeding your demons (a modern adaptation of Chöd)
practices.how: Find a struggle, such as fear or a craving, and feel where it lives in the body. Picture it as a figure in front of you and ask what it wants and what it really needs. Then imagine dissolving your body into nectar that gives it exactly that, until it is satisfied. Rest in the open space that remains.

practices.name: The view from above (spiritual exercise)
practices.how: In imagination, rise above your situation until your concerns appear in the scale of the cosmos; return with a lighter, more just sense of what matters. One of the ancient "spiritual exercises" Pierre Hadot described.

practices.name: Hermetic ascent and rebirth (Corpus Hermeticum XIII)
practices.how: Read slowly and as contemplation, not just as information: the treatise guides the reader to put away the "torments" of matter and be reborn as the intellect praising God in silence.

practices.name: Active imagination / imaginal attention
practices.how: Stay with an image (from a dream, a text or a place) as a living presence; let it speak and move; respond to it honestly rather than interpreting it away. In Corbin's terms it is a perception of the mundus imaginalis.
